10.summary: A cable tester checks a cable's continuity and pinouts: each end of the cable connects to a port on the tester, which shows the working conductive paths and the pin arrangements in the connectors.
10.deeper:
Hardware troubleshooting tools, as distinguished from software tools, are tools you can hold in your hand. A cable tester checks continuity and pinouts by connecting each end of the cable to the ports on the tester; it then displays the functional conductive paths and identifies the pin arrangements in the connectors. It is the tool that shows whether a cable is wired as intended.

Crimper: secures cable ends to connectors through the application of mechanical pressure, such as when attaching RJ-45 connectors to ethernet cables. The crimper builds the connection; the cable tester checks it.

Tone Generator: a handheld device, also known as a "Fox and Hound". It emits an audible tone (the fox) into one end of a cable while a probe with a sensor (the hound) detects the tone along the cable's length, aiding cable tracing and identification with sounds or lights that grow stronger as the probe approaches the cable.

Digital Multimeter: aids technicians in identifying faulty components or sections within malfunctioning circuits by testing parts of an electrical circuit with metal-tipped probes, measuring voltage, resistance and continuity.
10.analogy: A cable tester is like a teacher checking a seating chart: it looks at both ends of every wire and confirms that each one arrives at the seat it should.
10.scenario: An airman crimps RJ-45 connectors onto both ends of a new ethernet cable. Before using it, the airman plugs each end into a port on a cable tester, which shows that every conductive path works and that the pins are arranged as intended.
10.example: A string of holiday lights can be checked bulb by bulb to see that power reaches each one. In the course: Cable tester - checks continuity and pinouts of a cable by connecting each end of the cable to the ports on the tester, Study Guide p.99.

10.summary: An optical time domain reflectometer (OTDR) checks fiber optic cable for breaks: it sends a signal and measures the light reflected off a break, splice or defect, and it can estimate how far into the cable the defect is.
10.deeper:
An OTDR is a hardware troubleshooting tool for fiber. It checks for breaks in fiber optic cable by sending a signal and measuring the light that is reflected off the break, splice or defect in the fiber, and the test can determine the approximate distance into the cable for the defect. It is the fiber tool for finding where a fault is; copper cables are checked with tools such as a cable tester.

Optical Power Meter: works in conjunction with an optical light source to measure signal strength, to detect and measure excessive attenuation in fiber optic cables. The OTDR finds a break and its distance; the power meter measures how strong the light is.
10.analogy: An OTDR is like shouting down a long tunnel: the echo comes back from whatever blocks the tunnel, and it tells you roughly how far away the blockage is.
10.scenario: A fiber link between two buildings stops working. An airman connects an OTDR to one end; the reflected light shows a break and its approximate distance into the cable. On another fiber that works but is weak, the airman pairs an optical power meter with a light source to measure signal strength and find excessive attenuation.
10.example: An echo in a hallway comes back from the wall at its end. In the course: Optical Time Domain Reflectometer (OTDR) - Checks for breaks in fiber optic cable by sending a signal and measuring the light that is reflected off the break, splice, or defect in the fiber, Study Guide p.99.

10.summary: A protocol analyzer captures and analyzes individual packets to examine the information in them: source and destination addresses, protocols used, packet size and sometimes payload data.
10.deeper:
Software troubleshooting tools use command line inputs and applications at a computer workstation, or input to a network device through a console port. A protocol analyzer is one of them: it captures individual packets and analyzes them to examine information such as the protocols used, the source and destination addresses, the size of the packet and sometimes the payload data.

Port Scanner: identifies open virtual ports and services on a host, which is crucial for system security. Its use can range from legitimate security assessments to potential malicious exploitation. A protocol analyzer reads the packets that pass; a port scanner looks at what a host has open.

Bandwidth Speed Tester: measures internet connection speed by downloading and uploading sample files, calculating the speed in Mbps or Kbps and comparing it to expected speeds, which helps troubleshoot internet issues.
10.analogy: A protocol analyzer is like a mail sorter who opens each envelope's outside to read the sender, the address, the kind of mail and its size, and sometimes looks at the letter inside.
10.scenario: An airman troubleshoots slow traffic between a workstation and a server. A protocol analyzer captures packets on the link and shows each one's source and destination addresses, protocol and size. To check which ports and services the server has open, the airman would use a port scanner instead.
10.example: A customs officer opens a package to look at its label, its size and sometimes its contents. 10.summary: Ping troubleshoots network connectivity: it sends ICMP Echo Request messages to a destination host and analyzes the ICMP Reply results to find packet loss and latency.
10.deeper:
Ping is one of the command line inputs typed at the CMD prompt, a software troubleshooting tool. It is used for network connectivity issues: it sends ICMP Echo Request messages to a destination host, and the ICMP Reply results are analyzed to identify packet loss and latency.

Tracert: traces the network route from a source to a destination by sending ICMP Echo Request messages with varying Time-to-Live (TTL) values. Its results show the IP addresses of the routers encountered and the round-trip time (RTT) for each hop. Ping asks whether the host answers; tracert shows the path to it.

Nslookup: translates domain names to IP addresses and IP addresses back to domain names, a useful tool for network troubleshooting and DNS-related tasks.
10.analogy: Ping is like calling out "Can you hear me?" and timing the answer: no answer, or a slow one, tells you something is wrong on the way.
10.scenario: An airman cannot reach a server. Ping sends ICMP Echo Requests to it and shows packet loss and latency in the replies. To see where the trouble lies, tracert lists each router on the route and the round-trip time per hop. If the server's name will not resolve to an IP address, nslookup is the tool.
10.example: Knocking on a friend's door and waiting for an answer tells you whether anyone is home. In the course: ping - used for troubleshooting network connectivity issues by sending ICMP Echo Request messages to a destination host, Study Guide p.100.

10.summary: A connectivity test set checks for proper transmission (Tx) and reception (Rx) of data signals between devices in a network.
10.deeper: A connectivity test set works by sending a series of queries that determine and report information about a switch or device; that information is compared to advertised data rates and the results are given. It can also see whether data is streaming to and from the switch to each host, testing the cables between each device along the data paths. Some test sets are nothing more than fancy cable testers that check for continuity; others can test network connectivity and Power over Ethernet (PoE), and some can perform switch connectivity and Ping testing. When checking cables, some test sets are transmission testers that pass bits across the cable, while others evaluate the cable's physical qualities with a series of radio frequency (RF) tests, and the results are compared to the test limits IEEE 802.3 specifies for Ethernet.
10.analogy: A connectivity test set is like a doctor's check-up: it asks a series of questions, measures the answers and compares them with what healthy looks like.
10.scenario: A network printer is not printing what an airman's computer sends it. The airman unplugs the Ethernet cable from the back of the printer and plugs the same cable into a connectivity test set. The test set analyzes the data coming from the network to see whether it is consistent and strong enough for the printer to use.
10.example: A doctor listens to a heartbeat to check that it is steady and strong. In the course: Network connectivity test sets are used to test for proper transmission and reception of data communication signals between devices within a network, Study Guide p.101.

11.summary: A Network Monitoring System (NMS) monitors the network for problems caused by overloaded or crashed servers, network connections or other devices.
11.deeper:
The network is the lifeline of the IT infrastructure: when it fails, the flow of information that applications and business operations need stops. Network administrators typically use an NMS to monitor the availability of network services, the functionality of network interfaces, and the status of critical hardware, CPU, memory or bandwidth. NMSs also obtain other statistics: service or device availability, network response time and network route analytics. The NMS identifies and sends out alerts about issues affecting the availability or functionality of network services, which helps ensure critical systems are available and functioning properly.

Network monitoring also discovers suspicious and unauthorized access and activity on AF networks. Suspicious activity may include network scanning, multiple connection attempts to a network device from an unknown entity, or other reportable activity. Intrusion activity may include unusual or excessive activity on the network, or unauthorized individuals gaining full (root) or limited (user) access to a network device or information system. Examples of tools used are IDS and SNMP. An NMS provides five basic functions: Discover, Map, Monitor, Alert and Report; not all NMSs are alike, and they differ in the capabilities each function delivers.
11.analogy: An NMS is like a control tower for the network: it watches every aircraft, notices one that goes quiet or flies oddly, and warns the crews before trouble spreads.
11.scenario: An airman's NMS shows that a server has stopped responding to requests and sends an alert. The same morning it reports multiple connection attempts to a router from an unknown entity: suspicious activity, which the airman reports.
11.example: A building's security desk with cameras on every hallway notices a broken door or a stranger long before anyone calls. In the course: network monitoring systems monitor the network for problems caused by overloaded or crashed servers, network connections or other devices, Study Guide p.102.

11.summary: Discover is the first of the five NMS functions: it finds the devices on the network and, if it can, how they are connected.
11.deeper:
Network monitoring begins with the discovery process: if you don't know what's on the network and how it is all connected, you can't monitor it. NMSs discover the routers, switches, firewalls, servers, printers and more. They include a library of monitoring templates, which define how to monitor a device. When an NMS completes the discovery process, it automatically assigns an appropriate device role to each device on the discovered device list. Device roles are type and vendor specific: what you monitor on a Cisco router differs from a Dell server.

All NMSs discover devices, but not all discover how devices are connected: an NMS may identify a server without knowing which switch it is connected to. An NMS with Layer 2 or 3 discovery finds the port-to-port connectivity between devices. That matters because a performance problem on one device can impact another; when a switch fails, all devices connected to it can't communicate. That is why mapping, the next function, is required.
11.analogy: Discover is like taking roll on the first day: you list who is in the room and give each person a role before you can keep an eye on anyone, and the best roll also notes who sits next to whom.
11.scenario: An airman points a new NMS at the network. It finds the routers, switches, servers and printers and gives each a device role suited to its type and vendor. Because this NMS has Layer 2 or 3 discovery, it also learns which switch port each server connects to, ready for mapping.

11.summary: Monitor is the NMS function that keeps an eye on the network; NMSs provide turn-key device roles that define what to monitor.
11.deeper:
Network administrators can modify the device roles or create new ones from scratch, and NMSs offer a large selection of monitors. As a starting point, administrators want to monitor the "big 5" for any device on the network: ping availability and latency, CPU, memory, disk, and interface utilization. A ping is one of the most basic techniques monitoring software uses to test devices within a network.

Beyond the big 5, most network monitoring tools provide monitors for other hardware components, like the fans and power supplies in a switch, and can even monitor the temperature in a wiring closet. They can also monitor network services such as HTTP, TCP/IP and FTP.
11.analogy: Monitor is like a nurse's regular rounds: the same five vital signs for every patient first, then extra checks for the patients and rooms that need them.
11.scenario: An airman sets up monitoring for a new server. The device role starts the big 5: ping availability and latency, CPU, memory, disk and interface utilization. For the switch in the wiring closet, the airman adds monitors for its fans and power supplies and for the closet's temperature, and monitors the web server's HTTP service as well.
11.example: A car's dashboard gauges for speed, fuel and engine temperature keep an eye on the car while it runs. In the course: the Monitor function keeps an eye on your network, Study Guide p.105.

11.summary: Alert is the NMS function that notifies network administrators when something goes wrong; NMSs deliver alerts via email, text and logging.
11.deeper:
Threshold-based alerting enables network administrators to respond to problems before they impact users or applications. For example, the NMS is configured to issue an alert when the CPU utilization on a router exceeds 80%, so the administrator can investigate and respond before the router fails altogether.

Performance metrics such as CPU, memory and interface utilization fluctuate during the day and may exceed thresholds for a few seconds or minutes during peak usage. Administrators don't want to be bothered with these minor blips, so NMS alerts are configured with a time element: for instance, an alert is issued only if CPU utilization exceeds 80% for more than 10 minutes. Some NMSs also allow blackout periods, when alerts are suspended: printers shut down at night to save energy costs can have their alerts suspended during those hours.

Syslog: an automated messaging system that sends messages when an event affects a network device.
11.analogy: An NMS alert is like a smoke detector with sense: it ignores a brief puff from the toaster (a time element), stays quiet while the kitchen is closed for the night (a blackout period), but sounds when smoke keeps building.
11.scenario: An NMS watches a router's CPU utilization. At lunchtime it jumps over 80% for a few seconds and falls back; no alert. Later it stays over 80% for more than 10 minutes, and an alert reaches the administrator by text. The office printers, shut down every night, are in a blackout period, so their alerts are suspended.
11.example: A car's warning light that comes on only when the engine stays hot, not for a brief climb up a hill, warns early without crying wolf. In the course: the NMSs notify network administrators when something goes wrong, Study Guide p.105.

11.summary: Dashboards are the webpages in which NMSs deliver monitoring information; they are made up of turn-key views.
11.deeper:
Dashboards belong to the Report function, which deals with real-time and historical reporting. That data lets network administrators validate that network designs are delivering the desired results, expose trends that could impact the network's ability to deliver the performance users, applications and the mission demand, and isolate and fix performance problems quickly.

The turn-key views a dashboard is made of include, for example, a Top 10 CPU utilization view or a Top 10 Memory utilization view. Administrators scan summary dashboards to assess the health of the entire network, then drill down with detailed dashboards of specific devices and monitors to quickly isolate performance problems. Most NMSs are customizable: administrators can create dashboards for the Help Desk and for counterparts managing systems and applications.
11.analogy: Dashboards are like the instrument panel of a car: one glance shows whether everything is fine, and a closer look at one gauge shows where the trouble is.
11.scenario: An airman scans the summary dashboard each morning to check the health of the whole network. One device shows up in the Top 10 CPU utilization view, so the airman drills down into that device's detailed dashboard to isolate the performance problem.
11.example: A weather website that shows a national map first and lets you click into one city's forecast works the same way, from overview to detail. In the course: NMSs deliver monitoring information in webpages called dashboards, Study Guide p.106.

11.summary: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) detects anomalies with the aim of catching hackers before they do real damage to a network.
11.deeper: An IDS is placed on the network to monitor the traffic traversing it. IDSs scan, audit and monitor the security infrastructure for signs of attacks in progress. They work in two ways: by looking for signatures of known attacks, or by looking for deviations from normal activity. When an IDS finds signs of an attack, it alerts system administrators that an attack may be happening. IDSs are one of the tools used in network monitoring, alongside SNMP.
11.analogy: An IDS is like a security camera operator at a gate: they know the faces on the wanted list, they notice anyone acting unusually, and they radio the guards when something looks like trouble.
11.scenario: An IDS on a base network sees traffic that matches the signature of a known attack and alerts the system administrators. Later it sees traffic that matches no known signature but is far from normal activity; it flags that too, so the administrators can act before real damage is done.
11.example: A bank alarm that rings when someone opens the vault outside business hours catches unusual activity before money leaves the building. In the course: an IDS detects anomalies with the aim of catching hackers before they do real damage to a network, Study Guide p.107.

11.summary: The SNMP manager, within the NMS, is responsible for establishing communications with the SNMP agents, so the network administrator need not communicate directly with each individual device.
11.deeper:
SNMP is one of the most widely used protocols for monitoring: it collects data from almost any network-attached device, including routers, switches, wireless LAN controllers, wireless access points, servers and printers. The key functions of the SNMP management tool are querying agents, getting replies from agents, establishing variables in agents, and recognizing asynchronous events. The NMS navigates and manages the system, compiling, storing and requesting status information. SNMP works by querying objects: querying the CPU utilization object returns a value the NMS uses for alerting and reporting. Combined with an NMS, SNMP lets administrators view, monitor and manage the nodes through one interface, with batch command and automatic alert functions, instead of logging into each node by hand.

SNMP agent: most network devices today have SNMP agents installed in them; the SNMP software agents respond to the NMS's requests. Agents and the NMS communicate in the SNMP common language, which can provide key information on configuration changes and statuses. The manager asks; the agent in the device answers.
11.analogy: An SNMP manager is like a dispatcher with a radio to every truck: instead of driving out to each truck, the dispatcher calls, and the radio in each truck (the agent) answers with its status.
11.scenario: An airman manages hundreds of devices. Rather than logging into each, the NMS's SNMP manager queries the agent in each router for its CPU utilization. Each agent replies with the value, and the NMS uses it for alerting and reporting.
11.example: A teacher taking attendance by calling names, each student answering "here", gets the status of the whole room without walking to every desk. In the course: within the NMS, the SNMP manager is responsible for establishing communications with the SNMP agents, Study Guide p.107.

11.summary: A Management Information Base (MIB) maintains the objects that SNMP queries; it defines all the information exposed by the managed device.
11.deeper:
SNMP works by querying objects; an object is something an NMS collects information about. CPU utilization is an SNMP object: querying it returns a value the NMS uses for alerting and reporting. The objects queried by SNMP are maintained in a MIB. For example, the MIB for a Cisco router contains all objects defined by Cisco that can be used to monitor that router, such as CPU utilization, memory utilization and interface status.

The objects in a MIB are catalogued using a standardized numbering system, and each object has its own unique Object Identifier (OID). Some NMSs provide a MIB Browser, which lets network administrators navigate through a MIB to find additional objects they want to monitor on a device.
11.analogy: A MIB is like a library catalogue for one device: it lists every item the device can report on, and each item has its own call number (the OID) so it can be found exactly.
11.scenario: An airman wants to watch a router's interface status, which the NMS does not monitor yet. Using the NMS's MIB Browser, the airman navigates the router's MIB, finds the interface status object with its own OID, and adds it to the monitors.
11.example: A parts catalogue that gives every part of a machine its own part number lets a mechanic order exactly the right one. In the course: a MIB defines all the information that is exposed by the managed device, Study Guide p.107.
